title: A one-dimensional smooth connected unipotent group is additive
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes and homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme], closed subgroups as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], smoothness as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme], and finite type as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Write $\mathbf G_a$ and $\mathbf G_m$ for the group schemes of [def-sc-gm-ga]. The Lie algebra of a group is its tangent space at the identity [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. A smooth affine group is unipotent if every geometric point is a unipotent matrix in a faithful finite-dimensional linear representation. Let $U$ be a smooth connected affine unipotent $F$-group scheme of finite type. If $\dim_F\operatorname{Lie}(U)=1$, then there is an isomorphism of $F$-group schemes $\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U$. No restriction on the characteristic of $F$ is imposed.

source.place: Paragraph 14.58, printed p.298 (the classification of smooth connected one-dimensional unipotent groups over a perfect field); Proposition 1.37, printed p.18, identifies dimension with tangent dimension for a smooth group. The field here is algebraically closed, hence perfect.

proof.text: The field $F$ is perfect: in characteristic $p>0$, every polynomial $X^p-b$ has a root by [def-weil-algebraic-closure], so every $b\in F$ is a $p$-th power. Also $U$ is nontrivial. Indeed the trivial group $\operatorname{Spec}F$ has just one tangent vector, since there is just one $F$-morphism $\operatorname{Spec}F[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)\to\operatorname{Spec}F$; hence its tangent space has dimension zero by [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space], contradicting the given dimension one.

source.place: Paragraph 14.58, printed p.298: perfect-field hypothesis; elementary verification of nontriviality from the tangent dimension

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-unipotent-central-additive-subgroup] to $V=U$ over $F$. The required perfectness and nontriviality were checked in step 1; smoothness, connectedness, affineness, finite type and unipotence are hypotheses of the item. Obtain a smooth connected closed subgroup $N\subseteq U$ and an isomorphism $a:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}N$. Write $i:N\hookrightarrow U$ for the inclusion.

source.place: Corollary 14.55, printed p.297; characteristic-zero central-series argument in the proof of Proposition 14.32, printed p.289

proof.text: By [def-sc-gm-ga], $\mathbf G_a=\operatorname{Spec}F[y]$ and its identity is $y=0$ (the counit $\varepsilon(y)=0$). Its tangent vectors are exactly the $F$-algebra maps $F[y]\to F[\epsilon]$, $y\mapsto c\epsilon$, $c\in F$; the addition and scalar multiplication of [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space] identify this tangent space linearly with $F$. Postcomposition with $a$ and $a^{-1}$ gives inverse linear tangent maps, so $\operatorname{Lie}(N)$ has dimension one. By [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], $i(R)$ is injective for every $F$-algebra $R$, in particular $R=F[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. The tangent map $di$ is its restriction to vectors at the identity, hence injective. Therefore its image is a one-dimensional subspace of the one-dimensional $\operatorname{Lie}(U)$, and equals that space.

source.place: Proposition 1.37, printed p.18, and Corollary 10.17, printed p.191: elementary dual-number verification of the tangent-span hypothesis

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation] with $G=U$, a singleton family $H_1=N$, and $K=N$. The subgroup is smooth and connected by step 2. That lemma writes $\operatorname{Lie}=(\mathfrak m_e/\mathfrak m_e^2)^\vee$ with the dual of the cotangent map as differential; by [lem-sc-rational-tangent-cotangent-duality], applied to $i$ at the $F$-rational identity points, this is identified with the dual-number tangent space and tangent map of step 3, so its tangent image spans by step 3. Its inclusion factors through $K$ by the identity. The cited conclusion gives $N=U$ as closed subgroup schemes. Consequently the composite $i\circ a:\mathbf G_a\to U$ is an isomorphism of $F$-group schemes, as required.

source.place: Corollary 10.17 and its proof, printed p.191; conclusion of Paragraph 14.58, printed p.298

proof_origin.place: Assembly of Corollary 14.55 (and Proposition 14.32 proof in characteristic zero) with Corollary 10.17, using explicit dual-number tangent calculations; proves the converse in Paragraph 14.58 without introducing a dimension-to-Lie bridge.
